# Summary and questions

IQP (Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial-time) circuits are a restricted class of quantum circuits where all gates commute, equivalently described as $H^{\otimes n} D H^{\otimes n}$ where $D$ is a diagonal unitary.

- The seminal work [@bremner2011classical] was the first to show that this subclass already possesses multiplicative-error hardness.
- Moreover, $\log n$-depth non-local gates also suffice for supremacy [@bremner2016sparse] while local restriction enhanced the gate depth to $\sqrt{n} \log n$.
- Furthermore, adding intermediate measurements makes IQP universal [@jozsa2024iqp], so once IQP sampling is achieved, the techniques extend to universal computation. 

## IQP to BQP via Post-Selection

As a subset of universal circuits, IQP is remarkably close to full quantum computation. The key insight is that **post-selected IQP equals post-selected BQP**.

<!-- TODO: Figure showing IQP-to-BQP post-selection equivalence (original figure from external source) -->

::: {#thm-post-iqp .callout-important icon="false"}
## Post-Selection Universality of IQP

If a computational model equals post-BQP under post-selection, then no efficient classical multiplicative-error weak simulation exists [@bremner2011classical, Theorems 1--2].
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof (Click to expand)

*Proof.* If $\text{post-IQP}_{1,2}(\pi/8) = \text{post-BQP}$, then any weak simulation of all $\text{IQP}_{1,2}(\pi/8)$ circuits (with multiplicative error $1 \leq c < \sqrt{2}$) would imply $\text{post-BQP} = \text{post-IQP}_{1,2}(\pi/8) \subseteq \text{post-BPP}$.

Then $\text{post-BQP} = \text{post-BPP} = \text{PP}$. Further: $\text{PH} \subseteq \mathsf{P}^{\text{PP}} = \mathsf{P}^{\text{post-BPP}} \subseteq \mathsf{P}^{\Delta_3} = \Delta_3$.

Therefore, no classical algorithm can efficiently perform multiplicative-error weak simulation of all circuits composed of $P_j(\theta) = e^{i(\pi/8)Z_j}$ and $R_{jk}(\theta) = e^{i(\pi/8)Z_j \otimes Z_k}$, i.e., $\text{IQP}_{1,2}(\pi/8)$. $\square$
:::

Moreover, post-selection is not physically realizable. However, **adding intermediate measurements makes IQP universal** [@jozsa2024iqp]:

<!-- TODO: Figure showing IQP with intermediate measurements becoming universal (original figure from external source) -->

This also implies that if one can find an error-correcting code with transversal $\{CCZ\}$ gates and the ability to fault-tolerantly prepare $|0/1\rangle_L$, $|+/-\rangle_L$ and fault-tolerantly measure $|0/1\rangle_L$, $|+/-\rangle_L$, then universal fault-tolerant computation is possible without magic state distillation.

## Average-Case Hardness

In real experimnent, 
there exists many randomized methods that can be chosen to set up an IQP-circuit ensembles.
Each such randomized method will induce certain average-case problems.
The anti-concentration and hiding properties are then proved/numerically verified for each randomized method.


#### Degree-based

The gate set writes $\{\mathrm{Z}, \mathrm{CZ}, \mathrm{CCZ}, \cdots, \mathrm{C}^k\mathrm{Z}\}$, which we called the k-degree IQP circuits. 
This gate sets require $k$-body interactions, which is hard to realized in simulation-based experiment while can be realized in fault-tolerant/digital quantum computers.

Consider an IQP circuit $C$ generated by $\{\mathrm{Z}, \mathrm{CZ}, \mathrm{CCZ}\}$,
with $c_i,b_{ij},a_{ijk} \in \mathbb{F}_2$ indicates the existence of those gates on qubit tumples $(i),(ij),(ijk)$, respectively.
Then probability of this IQP instance measuring outcome $\vec{s}$ is:
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{Pr}(C) &= \frac{1}{2^n} \sum_{z \in \{0,1\}^n} \langle z|(-1)^{z \cdot s} \sum_{x \in \{0,1\}^n} (-1)^{f_C(x)} |x\rangle \\
&= \frac{1}{2^n} \sum_{z \in \{0,1\}^n} (-1)^{z \cdot s} (-1)^{f_C(z)} =: \text{ngap}[f_C(z) + z \cdot s],\\
f_C(z) &= \sum_i c_i z_i + \sum_{ij} b_{ij} z_i z_j + \sum_{ijk} a_{ijk} z_i z_j z_k.
\end{align*}
$$
Since there are only polynomially many gates, $f_C(z)$ is degree-3 boolean functions with polynomially many monomials, thus been efficiently computable.

:::{#thm-gap3 .callout-note icon = "false"}

#### Rotation-based

The gate set writes  $\{\mathrm{diag}(1,1,1,e^{i\theta_{jk}}), \mathrm{diag}(1,e^{i\varphi_j})\}$, with $\theta_{jk}, \varphi_{j} \in [0, 2\pi)$.
This gate sets require small single qubit $Z$-rotating gates and two-body interactions, thus can be realized on a simulation-based Hamiltonian with $K_{jk} t = \theta_{jk}, h_j t = \varphi_j$:
$$
U_{\rm Ry}(t) = \exp\left[i\sum_{j<k} K_{jk}t\, Z_jZ_k + i\sum_j h_j t\, Z_j\right].
$$
Since no transversal gates, the probability of this IQP instance measuring outcome $\vec{s}$ is:
$$
Z(\omega) = \sum_{z \in \{\pm 1\}} \omega^{\sum_{i<j} q_{i,j} z_i z_j + \sum_k v_k z_k},
$$
where $\omega = e^{i\pi/8}$, and $q_{i,j}, v_k \in \{0, \ldots, 7\}$ correspond to $\{CZ, CS\}$ phase gates between qubits $i,j$ and $\{Z, S, T\}$ phase gates on qubit $k$.


::: {#thm-ising-gapp .callout-important icon="false"}

Computing all Ising partition functions is a GapP-complete problem. [todo: make this statement more concrete]

\begin{align*}

&\{\mathrm{diag}(1,e^{il\pi/4})\},l \in 0\cdots,7.
  \end{align*}
$$
